title: Shavuot: a wedding at the mountain
hook: the rabbis picture Sinai as a wedding, the mountain held over the people like a canopy

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jerusalem and Psalm 122. Your line was pray for jerusalem's peace. Did the line come to you during the day? Today, the count of the Omer ends, and we arrive at the mountain. Day six hundred ninety.

At a Jewish wedding, the couple stands under a chuppah: a canopy, often just a prayer shawl or a cloth held up on four poles. A document is read, the ketubah, spelling out promises. Words are spoken. Something is given. And then a crowd that was holding its breath bursts into song. Now picture another scene. A mountain covered in cloud and smoke, thunder, a horn growing louder and louder, a whole people gathered at its foot. On Shavuot, Jews celebrate that day at Sinai. And for many centuries, teachers have said that what happened there was a wedding.
screen: `A CANOPY, A DOCUMENT, A PROMISE.` → `A MOUNTAIN IN SMOKE AND THUNDER.` → `WHAT IF IT WAS A WEDDING?`

segments.voice: Shavuot means weeks: the festival at the end of the seven weeks of counting. In the Torah it's a harvest feast, the first wheat. The rabbis tied it to the giving of the Torah at Sinai. And the wedding picture has old roots. The Mishnah, at the end of tractate Taanit, reads a verse from the Song of Songs about King Solomon's wedding day and says: that's the giving of the Torah. God is the groom, Israel the bride. The Torah's own description of the day invites the comparison. In the old Jewish translation: "And Moses brought forth the people out of the camp to meet God; and they stood at the nether part of the mount." At the bottom of the mountain. But the Hebrew can also be read: underneath the mountain. The Talmud, in Shabbat 88a, takes that literally, and here the honest thing is to say the image isn't gentle. God, it says, held the mountain over them like an overturned barrel, and said: if you accept the Torah, good; if not, here will be your grave. The Talmud itself is uneasy, and adds that the people later accepted it fully, freely, in the days of Esther. Later teachers took the same picture and softened it: the mountain overhead became the wedding canopy. And at the foot of it, the people's answer, which the Torah gives: All that the LORD has spoken, we will do. Many Sephardi communities read an actual marriage contract on Shavuot morning, a ketubah between God and Israel, written by a sixteenth-century poet. A wedding at the mountain: a promise made under a canopy of cloud.
screen: `SHAVUOT: THE FEAST OF WEEKS.` · `THE DAY OF HIS WEDDING.` · `UNDER THE MOUNTAIN.` · `A KETUBAH FOR SHAVUOT.` · then, large: `A WEDDING AT THE MOUNTAIN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: reread a promise you made. If you have one written down, wedding vows, a letter, a commitment you signed, an old journal entry, find it, and read it slowly. If not, remember one, word for word if you can. Breathe. Ask yourself, without judgment: how is this promise doing? What would it look like to make it again, freely, today? The bell holds the time.
Shavuot. Weeks: the festival at the end of the Omer, remembered as the day of Sinai, a wedding at the mountain. Today's word.
Your line: a wedding at the mountain. Today, renew one promise, out loud, to the person you made it to. Day six hundred ninety.

howItsDone: On Shavuot, many Jews stay up through the night studying Torah, hear the Ten Commandments read in the synagogue, and in many Sephardi communities, a ketubah for Shavuot is read, portraying Sinai as the marriage of God and Israel.

original.note: Hebrew: weeks, for the seven weeks counted from Passover.

trapdoor: what you thought: Shavuot is a harvest holiday.
what it means: it's also the day of Sinai, pictured as a wedding between God and Israel.
what a scholar hears: Mishnah Taanit 4:8 reads Song of Songs 3:11 as Sinai; Shabbat 88a's overturned mountain; Israel Najara's ketubah for Shavuot.

sources.quoted: And Moses brought forth the people out of the camp to meet God; and they stood at the nether part of the mount.

notes: Exodus 19:17 quoted from JPS 1917 from memory; verify.
Exodus 19:8 / 24:7 answer paraphrased in modern English ('we will do') rather than quoted.
Shabbat 88a: Rav Avdimi bar Chama's barrel image; Rava's 'they re-accepted it in the days of Ahasuerus' (Esther 9:27). Paraphrased.
The canopy (chuppah) reading of the overturned mountain is a later homiletic softening; source not pinned to one author. Check.
Ketubah for Shavuot attributed to Israel Najara (16th century); verify.
